{
  "analyses": [
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-1145-1082473-1082754",
      "title": "Layered message semantics using social commitments",
      "research_question": "How can message semantics in open multiagent systems be grounded in publicly observable social commitments and conversational context rather than relying primarily on unverifiable private mental states?",
      "methodology": "The paper develops a conceptual commitment-based semantics inspired by social-commitment models and theories of language use. It defines commitment states and transitions and then organizes message meaning into four incremental layers: compositional, conversational, commitment-state, and joint-activity semantics. The authors illustrate the higher layers with a contract-net interaction involving manager and bidder roles rather than conducting an empirical evaluation.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The proposed semantics decomposes message interpretation into four cumulative levels: compositional structure, conversational use, commitment state, and joint activity.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 2, Commitment-Based Model"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Social commitments provide publicly represented states including inactive, accepted or active, fulfilled, violated, and cancelled states, with adoption, fulfillment, violation, and discharge as relevant transitions.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 1.1, Social Commitments"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Conversational meaning depends on the temporal and sequential context of shared utterances, including whether a proposal remains available for a reply.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 2.2, Conversational Level"
        },
        {
          "finding": "At the commitment-state level, the same structural message can receive a more specific interpretation according to the current state of the referenced commitment, such as an offer withdrawal when an active commitment is proposed for discharge by the original offering agent.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 2.3, Commitment State Level"
        },
        {
          "finding": "At the joint-activity level, message meaning is related to role-specific actions and their dependencies, as illustrated by bid production, bid evaluation, and contract performance in a contract-net activity.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 2.4, Joint Activity Level"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The authors position signal meaning based on public coordination as a complement to speaker-intention semantics whose use in open systems otherwise depends on assumptions about agent sincerity.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 3, Conclusions"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The paper is primarily a conceptual model and presents no empirical comparison or experimental validation.",
        "The treatment explicitly concentrates on communications that make commitments accepted or rejected and does not model fulfillment and violation transitions arising from satisfaction conditions in comparable detail.",
        "A more detailed description of the model is deferred to separate work cited by the authors.",
        "The model represents current conversational, commitment, and activity state but does not specify an explicit persistent history or versioning mechanism for superseded commitment states."
      ],

        "code_available": false,

        "Mental-state semantics are difficult to verify when independently designed agents interact in open systems.",

        "Joint-activity semantics associates messages with actions performed by agents in defined roles.",
        "The authors treat publicly observable signal meaning as useful for coordinating open multiagent interaction."

      "source_url": "https://www.researchgate.net/publication/221456697_Layered_message_semantics_using_social_commitments",
      "access": "full_text"
    },

      "paper_id": "doi-10-1007-3-540-44503-x-20",
      "title": "Why and Where: A Characterization of Data Provenance",
      "research_question": "How can the provenance of query-produced data be formally characterized and computed in terms of both why an output exists and where its values originated, while remaining meaningful under query rewriting and view composition?",
      "methodology": "The paper uses a formal database-theory methodology based on a deterministic semistructured data model with explicit source locations and a query language called DQL. It defines normal forms and a rewrite system, then formalizes why-provenance through witnesses and witness bases and where-provenance through source paths and derivation bases. The authors prove normalization, soundness, completeness, invariance, and query-composition results and use worked relational and hierarchical-data examples rather than empirical experiments.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The paper distinguishes why-provenance, which identifies source data responsible for an output's existence, from where-provenance, which identifies source locations from which particular output values were obtained.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Sections 1 and 4, Introduction and Two Meanings of Provenance"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Every well-formed query in the defined language has an equivalent normal form reachable through a strongly normalizing rewrite system.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 3, A Query Language, Theorem 1"
        },
        {
          "finding": "For a normal-form query and singular output value, the proposed Why procedure computes the same witness basis as the formal provenance definition.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5.1, Witness Basis, Theorem 2"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Although a query-dependent witness basis is not invariant under all equivalent formulations, its minimal witness basis is invariant for equivalent well-formed queries restricted to equality conditions, with stated extensions to some inequality subclasses.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5.2, Minimal Witness Basis, Theorem 3"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Why-provenance can be propagated through materialized views so that recursively tracing witnesses through views agrees with composing the views out of the query.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5.3, Cascaded Witnesses, Theorem 4"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Where-provenance is not generally invariant under equivalent query rewritings, but the paper identifies a restricted class of traceable queries whose derivation basis is preserved by its rewrite system.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 6, Where-Provenance, Propositions 1 and 2"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The analysis is restricted to well-formed and well-defined queries under the paper's DQL assumptions.",
        "Variables are restricted to singular values, and DQL is explicitly less expressive than XML-QL in several respects, including lack of Kleene-star path patterns and limitations on nested-query and Skolem-function forms.",
        "A general semantic characterization of where-provenance is not established; rewrite invariance is obtained only for the restricted traceable-query class.",
        "The strongest minimal-witness invariance result is stated for equality conditions, with only some subclasses involving inequalities covered.",
        "Some XML translation and comparison details are deferred to a fuller version.",
        "The paper establishes formal properties but provides no empirical performance or scalability evaluation.",
        "The framework explains derivation provenance of query results rather than temporal version histories of corrections, supersessions, or reopened records."

        "traceable_where_invariance": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "Why-provenance concerns the source data whose presence accounts for an output's existence.",
        "Where-provenance concerns the source location or locations from which a particular output value was extracted.",
        "The deterministic data model gives every represented node a uniquely describable path.",
        "DQL can express positive select-project-join-union relational queries and positive nested relational algebra under the paper's restrictions.",
        "The rewrite system reaches a normal form from every well-formed query in finitely many rewrite steps.",
        "A witness is a source substructure sufficient for producing the output under the query.",
        "The Why procedure is sound and complete for the witness basis of normal-form queries and singular output values.",
        "Minimal witness bases are invariant across equivalent well-formed queries using equality conditions.",
        "Provenance traced through materialized views agrees with provenance after the views are composed out of the query.",
        "Where-provenance is more sensitive than why-provenance to the syntactic form of equivalent queries.",
        "For traceable queries, derivation bases used for where-provenance are preserved by the specified rewrite system."

      "source_url": "https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/opb/papers/ICDT2001.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-1023-a-1010318403544",
      "title": "The Problem of Retraction in Critical Discussion",
      "research_question": "What kind of dialogue model can permit retractions when they are reasonable or required while constraining or sanctioning retractions that would disrupt an orderly critical discussion?",
      "methodology": "The paper conducts a philosophical and normative analysis of commitment retraction in argumentative dialogue and expands earlier work on commitment in dialogue. It uses constructed dialogue examples to identify situations in which retraction is disruptive, permissible, or required, and derives design principles for retraction rules. It further classifies dialogue types and commitment types and proposes complex dialogue structures that can combine relatively permissive and rigorous retraction regimes.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Retraction changes a participant's current commitments rather than erasing the historical fact that an earlier utterance occurred, so adequate scorekeeping alone does not remove the problem caused by changing commitments on which another participant relied.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 1, The Problem"
        },
        {
          "finding": "A successful elementary critical discussion necessarily ends with at least one participant retracting a commitment, either the proponent's thesis or the opponent's doubt.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 1, The Problem"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Retraction rules should specify both which retractions are permissible in a given dialogical state and what consequences follow, including possible secondary retractions.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 2, Ingredients for a Solution"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Appropriate retraction rules depend on both the type of dialogue and the type of commitment, rather than being uniform across all conversations.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 2, Ingredients for a Solution"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Assertions and concessions carry different obligations, and a statement can in principle be retracted as an assertion while remaining available as a concession.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 2, Ingredients for a Solution"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Assertions are in principle retractable and may have to be retracted to resolve an inconsistency, with retraction potentially changing the outcome of the dispute.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 3.1, Assertions"
        },
        {
          "finding": "A complex dialogue can combine a permissive principal dialogue with rigorous subdialogues, allowing different retraction policies to apply in different parts of the same overall interaction.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 2, Ingredients for a Solution"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The author explicitly states that the proposed requirements cannot be proved absolutely necessary because the notion of a satisfactory implementation is itself vague.",

        "The detailed classification in Section 3 is restricted to light-side propositional commitments.",
        "Dark-side commitments can only be subjected to explicit retraction rules after they have been brought to light.",
        "The work is a normative and conceptual analysis based on constructed examples rather than an empirical study of real conversations.",

      "raw_claims": [
        "Frequent or strategically timed retractions can make an argumentative dialogue disorderly and ineffective.",
        "Recording that an earlier statement was uttered does not solve the separate problem that its speaker may later withdraw the associated commitment.",
        "Resolution of an elementary dispute requires either the proponent to abandon the thesis or the opponent to abandon doubt.",
        "A rational discussant may need to retract a position that cannot be defended against cogent counterargument.",
        "An exposed inconsistency can require withdrawal of at least one conflicting commitment.",
        "Dialogue rules should determine whether a particular retraction is allowed in the current situation.",
        "Rules should also determine what further commitment changes follow from an allowed retraction.",
        "Deliberation, inquiry, negotiation, and critical discussion can appropriately employ different retraction policies.",
        "Assertions carry a burden of defense whereas mere concessions do not.",
        "An utterance may lose its status as an assertion without necessarily losing its status as a concession.",
        "Light-side commitments arise overtly in dialogue while dark-side commitments are inferred from background or behavior.",
        "A dialogue architecture can embed strict subdialogues inside a more permissive principal dialogue."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://www.phil.uu.nl/ozsl/articles/krabbe03.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-1016-j-ipm-2026-104709",
      "title": "HeterMV: Multi-view reasoning over source-aware heterogeneous evidence graph for multi-source fact verification",
      "research_question": "Can explicit source-aware heterogeneous graph modeling and multi-view evidence reasoning improve multi-source fact verification while suppressing irrelevant, redundant, or inconsistent auxiliary evidence?",
      "methodology": "HeterMV represents core evidence, surrounding context, and reference documents as distinct node types in a source-aware heterogeneous evidence graph and uses directed multi-relational propagation to aggregate auxiliary information toward core evidence. It constructs four reasoning views—multi-source fusion, core-corroboration, context-infusion, and knowledge-citation—and combines view-conditioned prompt tuning with cross-view consistency contrastive learning. The model is evaluated against state-of-the-art baselines on the public Check-COVID and FEVEROUS-S datasets using both gold-evidence and BM25-retrieval settings, with comparative evaluation, ablation studies, hyperparameter analysis, and case analysis described in the accessible preview.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The framework explicitly preserves source roles by representing core evidence, context, and reference documents as different node types and by using source-specific directed relations rather than homogenizing all evidence.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Abstract and Methodology"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Four decoupled reasoning views are used to separate evidence perspectives, while view-conditioned prompt tuning aligns each perspective with the claim and cross-view contrastive learning is intended to reinforce supportive signals and suppress noisy ones.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Abstract and Methodology"
        },
        {
          "finding": "On Check-COVID with 1,504 claims, HeterMV reports Micro-F1 improvements of 3.06 percentage points in the gold setting and 3.27 percentage points under BM25 retrieval over the compared state-of-the-art baselines.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Abstract and Experiments"
        },
        {
          "finding": "On FEVEROUS-S with 29,890 claims, HeterMV reports Micro-F1 improvements of 1.72 percentage points in the gold setting and 1.41 percentage points in the corresponding BM25-retrieval setting.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Abstract and Experiments"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The accessible article preview reports that ablation studies validate contributions from the framework's major components and that the evaluation also includes hyperparameter-sensitivity and case analyses.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Contributions and Experiments"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The method is explicitly scoped to three forms of textual evidence—core evidence, local context, and reference documents—even though fact-verification evidence can also include tables, images, and knowledge graphs.",
        "The reported evaluation is limited to two benchmark datasets, Check-COVID and FEVEROUS-S, so behavior outside those benchmark settings is not established by the accessible material.",
        "Only an article preview and abstract-level material were accessible, so detailed per-class results, full ablation values, failure cases, and any author-stated limitations could not be independently inspected.",
        "No public code repository was identifiable in the accessible article material."

        "HeterMV treats core evidence, context, and reference documents as semantically different evidence sources.",
        "Directed multi-relational propagation aggregates auxiliary evidence into representations centered on core evidence.",
        "The framework reasons through multi-source fusion, core-corroboration, context-infusion, and knowledge-citation views.",

    }
